messages.subject: Stratified Sampling Design
parts:
Hello,

For my thesis I'm helping with my state wildlife agency's (Texas) redesign of their annual survey for white-winged dove. The ecology of the species has shifted and white-wings now occupy (almost) exclusively urban areas across the entire state as opposed to open woodlands in South Texas. They will venture outside of cities during the day, but for nesting and roosting, they stay within urban areas. As such, the state designed their original survey in 2008 using a stratified design that targets the larger cities. The point placement process used a 500m grid with points at each intersection, points greater than 100m from a public road were removed and those remaining were snapped to the nearest road (and yes I know this biases estimates but biologists can't go traipsing through homeowner's backyards). Each year, a selection of cities (usually around 200) are sampled once via point counts. The number of points varies between cities depending on the size but the lowest number of points is 10 and the largest is 180. In any given year, there are 266 cities that can be surveyed; 156 have 15 points and 43 have 30 just to give you an idea of the scope of the survey. 

After 9 years of the survey, the state has decided they want to take more of a classical sampling approach by which they focus more effort on areas with higher abundance to increase the efficiency of the survey. I am now tasked with determining how many/which cities need to be surveyed and how many points each one of those cities must have to keep the variance on the statewide population estimate at an acceptable level. The focus is on statewide and regional abundances; the state isn't overly concerned with dove abundances at the city level (the regional level refers to a subpopulation analysis we did previously; there's 5 across the state of Texas). That being said, I have stratified my densities by each city so that I can attempt to extrapolate them to non-surveyed cities using covariates from a hierarchical model (another topic entirely). This is a necessary process as cities that are not surveyed account for approximately 18,100 of 43,500 square kilometers of potential dove habitat. Just using a rough population estimate from a CDS analysis and assuming densities of non-surveyed cities were the same as the average regional densities, these non-surveyed areas can inflate state abundance estimates by 5 million birds.

 So, onto the actual question... I apologize for the long setup. What is the best way to go about adjusting the number of points for a given city based on its density/abundance? I'm assuming that adjusting the number of points by city is the way to go since 1) white-winged dove do not occupy the space between cities and 2) obtaining density estimates by city is a necessary process so that we can extrapolate to non-surveyed areas using covariates.

 I know I could use the equation from 7.2.2.2 of the Introduction to Distance Sampling text to correct the number of points but I've run into some issues with some example calculations. In the following examples, I want to lower the CV to 0.2 and I assume b = 3:

Burnet, TX Estimates for 2016

cv_density=40.45; k_0= 14; n_0 = 10

k=(3/{0.2}^2)*(14/10)
k=105 points needed

but if the CV is already less than 0.2:

Winters, TX estimates for 2016

cv_density=17.61; k_0 = 15; n_0 = 35
k=32.14 points needed

Shouldn't the number of necessary points be lower since we have some room to spare?

In the Advanced Distance Sampling text, Section 7.2.1.4 references the Underwood (2004) dissertation which sounds like what I am trying to do (allocate points with probability proportional to expected density), however, I cannot find it online.

Another option that I suppose is possible but not necessarily "good" would be to calculate the number of points needed at the state or regional level to bring the CV to XX% and then allocating points (using the same placement system as the original survey) to the cities with largest abundances until we run out of points.

Does anyone have any recommendations?

Thanks in advance,

Conor McInnerney

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Stratified Sampling Design
parts:
Conor

A lot to chew on in your post.  I'll set aside your comments about inferences drawn to non-surveyed cities with your covariates.

In answer to your practical questions:

Regarding sample size calculations: as you note, the equations in Buckland et al. (2001) are based on the assumption of b=3.  In your example of Winters TX, where the formula produces an estimate of 32 point, whereas a CV of 0.18 was obtained with 15 points; the value of b in Winters was smaller than 3.

As for access to Dr. Underwood's dissertation, a link to all her publications can be found at

http://www.fmunderwood.com/publications/
